name: Takestani
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Yar-Shater, Ehsan 1969. A Grammar of Southern Tati Dialects (covers Takestani); also Taheri 1991 Dastur-e zaban-e Tati-ye Takestan. Not found online.

new_statements.quote: Stress is contrastive in Takestani words and partly predictable from word class and shape. Stress in nouns is generally ultimate (e.g., /peˈrʌ/ ‘brother’) unless in nouns ending with the feminine suffix -ɛ (e.g., /zɛjˈni.ɛ/ ‘woman’). Most adverbs and adjectives, like nouns, are stressed on their last syllable, such as [pøland-pøˈland] ‘loud-loud (loudly)’ and [qaˈʃank] ‘beautiful.’ [...] present tense verbs are generally stressed on their last syllable (e.g., [meχanˈte] ‘laugh.3SG.M.IND (He laughs)’, and past tense verbs are stressed on their stem /ʌˈχɑrtem/ ‘PV.drink.PST.1SG (I drank)’.
new_statements.citation: Taherkhani, Neda & Scott Nelson. 2024. Southern Tati: Takestani Dialect. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 54(1): 559-574. doi:10.1017/S0025100323000270
new_statements.locator: p. 567, section 'Prosody', subsection 'Stress' (PDF page 9 of the file); minimal pairs p. 570
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is on the final syllable (nouns, adjectives, adverbs, present-tense verbs); the feminine suffix -ɛ is unstressed so feminine nouns are stressed on the penult; past-tense verbs stress the stem; monosyllabic adpositions are clitics and unstressed. Stress is therefore morphologically conditioned and contrastive in a few morphological minimal pairs (/vɛˈjɛ/ 'wedding' vs /ˈvɛj-ɛ/ 'bride'; /uˈvaz/ 'dancer' vs /ˈuvaz/ 'dance!'), but the placement is predictable from word class and morphology. Yar-Shater 1969 (§§82-83, pp. 57-58) agrees for the whole Southern Tati group: 'All uninflected masculine nouns are stressed on the final syllable'; 'All plural oblique nouns are stressed on the final syllable'; stress 'distinctive' yet 'generally predictable', and 'weak and dominated by sentence stress and intonation'.
new_statements.exceptions: Feminine nouns in -ɛ (older -a) stressed on the penult; past-tense verbs stem-stressed; adpositions cliticized and unstressed; verb stress governed by 'stress-attracting morphemes that compete for stress in a hierarchy' (details declared beyond the study's scope); Yar-Shater 1969: compounds keep only the second member's stress; imperfect stresses the last syllable of the past stem.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress, with a note that at phrase level nouns attract stress and adjectives/adverbs are less prominent; Yar-Shater 1969 says word stress is weak and dominated by sentence stress and intonation. Acoustic cues (JIPA): higher f0 and intensity on stressed vowels; duration is not a cue (final lengthening instead).
new_statements.identity_note: The JIPA illustration describes the Takestani dialect of Southern Tati as spoken in the city of Takestan (Siyaden), Qazvin province — exactly Glottolog take1255 / ISO tks. Yar-Shater 1969 states its stress rules for 'Southern Tati' as a group (Chali, Takestani, Eshtehardi, Esfarvarini, Xiaraji, Xoznini, Danesfani, Ebrahimabadi, Sagzabadi) with Takestani examples; Glottolog/Ethnologue subsume this Ramand-Eshtehard group under take1255, so the two sources describe the same variety at different granularity.

sources.note: Section 'Prosody > Stress', p. 567: stress is contrastive but partly predictable from word class/shape; nouns generally ultimate except feminine-suffix -ɛ nouns (penult); adverbs/adjectives final; clitic adpositions unstressed; present-tense verbs final, past-tense verbs stem-stressed; acoustic study: f0 and intensity cue stress, duration does not (final lengthening); minimal pairs /vɛˈjɛ/ 'wedding' vs /ˈvɛj-ɛ/ 'bride', /uˈvaz/ 'dancer' vs /ˈuvaz/ 'dance!' (p. 570).

sources.citation: Yarshater, Ehsan. [1969]. The distinction of gender in Southern Tati. Offprint from Studia classica et orientalia Antonino Pagliaro oblata, vol. III.
sources.note: Footnote 1 (offprint p. [2]): 'In this paper a final -a is to be assumed unstressed unless marked otherwise. Words ending in unstressed -a have the stress on the penultimate syllable unless marked otherwise.' Also notes a few feminines in stressed -a and stressed -i. Implies default final stress; mainly Chali data with Takestani cognates.
No statement on stress; used only for its bibliography, which pointed to the JIPA illustration and to Taherkhani 2017 (NACIL abstract, link now 404).

Tak. vii(y)a "water", kasuya "turtle", fareka "chicken", hoya "stream"'; masc. sg. oblique ends in unstressed -e. No general stress rule stated.
